utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Morning ladies and gentlemen. Can we have the witness? Could you please invite the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honour pleases, for the Prosecution, my name is Niemann, and I appear with Mr. Turone and Ms. McHenry, and we are assisted at our table by Ms. Van Dusschoten. (Witness enters court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: May we have appearances for the Defence, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning your Honour, my name is Edina Residovic, I am Defence counsel for Mr. Zejnil Delalic. My co-counsel is Mr. Eugene O'Sullivan, Professor of Law from Canada.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your Honours, my name is Olujic, defence counsel for Mr. Mucic. With me in the team is my colleague Michael Greaves, attorney from the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARABDIC
utterances.text: Good morning, your honours, my name is Salih Karabdic. With me in the team is Mr. Thomas Moran, lawyer from Houston Texas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good morning your honours, I am John Ackerman. I appear on behalf of Mr. Esad Landzo, and with me is my co-counsel, Cynthia McMurray.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly remind the witness you are still under oath.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, you are still under oath. MILENKO KULJANIN (continued)

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, I should now like to go back to some questions that were discussed yesterday in the course of the examination-in-chief and the cross-examination by my colleagues. I think these will be questions that can very easily be answered because you have lived in Konjic for a long time and you are familiar with the conditions there. Have I made myself clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, Mr. Kuljanin, you said that you knew that the house of Mr. Zejnil Delalic was situated on the road leading out of Konjic to Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also stated that in that house there used to be a car wash service or a car maintenance shop as you said; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You confirmed in this courtroom that you knew that on the ground floor of this house, a modern discotheque had been built and had functioned there before the war, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, you also said that earlier, you yourself personally had visited the car repair shop and especially the discotheque, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that sometimes in view of your occupation and the discotheque's needs, you had provided beer for the discotheque?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe you did not understand me, I accompanied my colleague who was supplying the discotheque with beer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification, I obviously did not understand you quite well. Now it is quite clear. Since I have now repeated in order to verify whether I understood properly what you said yesterday, I am sure you will agree with me if I say that even before the war, you knew very well where Mr. Delalic's house stood and that you were able to describe it, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, Mr. Kuljanin, you did not need the war nor to spend time in Celebici to be able to tell anyone who would ask you where that house is and what it contained, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As both of us knows, further details regarding the position of the house, but for the benefit of the court I would like to ask you to clear up a few more details with me. You said that viewing the house from the direction of Sarajevo or Konjic, the main road from Konjic to Mostar passes the house on the right-hand side of the house if you are going from Sarajevo, then the house is on the right. Right of the house is the main road and on the left is the Nerveta river?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you are going along the main road from Sarajevo to Mostar the house is on the right-hand side, and next to the house also on the right-hand side is the Nerveta river.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the left side of the house is the main highway?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Both the house and the road are situated under a steep slope, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You know, Mr. Kuljanin, that particularly in the autumn and in the spring but also in the event of heavy rains in Konjic, there may be a great deal of water, mud and stones coming from that slope; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also know that if that occurs the traffic gets jammed on this highway because there is no other road leading in or out of Konjic, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You are also aware, Mr. Kuljanin, that in such a situation the public maintenance service in charge of sanitation and hygiene take steps to clear the road of the mud and the pebbles and stones, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, under normal conditions of life that was so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That is what I am asking you. There is debris collects on the road, it also spreads to a part of the garden or front garden of Mr. Delalic, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, the situation was rather like that, was it not, when you visited this region as regards the debris, the mud and the stones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, there were quite a lot of troops there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in the yard.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were talking also about the arrest of Juka Prazina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had not heard about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that time when you visited the house you saw nobody but the troops?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only the security guards who were watching the garden, the yard and the house.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuljanin, we have now clarified the circumstances that you referred to before this Tribunal yesterday. I would now like to go back to Bradina and the period of time you testified about, but to look into some details which have not been cleared up so far, namely you said that the combat operations on May 5th when they broke out, you were in Bradina, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that a day later or 24 hours later into the combat operations, you decided to retreat in the direction of Jasica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did flee from the onslaught of Muslim units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that in Jasica you met Momir Mrkajic, Brano Gligorevic and Milovan Gligorevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those are all your neighbours from Bradina or the region of Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you decided to cross into areas under the control of the Serb forces with these neighbours of yours, you intended to go to Hadzici by crossing Mount Bjelijasinca?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have a clear idea of where we wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But on that day in the hamlet of Jasica, in the house of Mirko Dordic, you met your neighbour Zara Mrkajic 6?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, at that same spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You then learned from Zara Mrkajic that Rajko Dordic with another group of people, local people, was also leaving Bradina in the direction of Borci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had heard that they were moving somewhere, but Zara did not tell us in which direction and we did not know in which direction.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: With this group, which included Rajko Dordic, you met up with this group in the village of Laniste?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is not a village, it is a mountain and that is where we met.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You met there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but by chance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then you decided to try and proceed together to try to reach Borci?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I am correct, and I may be refreshing your memory when I give you the names of the people, in the group in addition to yourself were the following people, Rajko Dordic, Dragan Vujicic, somebody called Kulas from Tarcin whose name I do not know, then another young man from Tarcin known as Jacor, Zara Mrkajic, Branislav Gligorevic, Milovan Gligorevic, Momir Mrkajic, Rajko Kuljanin, Jelenko Kuljanin, Velimir Kuljanin, Milovan Kuljanin, Snjezan Gligorevic, Mladen Gligorevic, known as Hasko, Aleksa Gligorevic and some others whose name I am not familiar. Have I listed correctly a certain number of people who were with you in the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You enumerated roughly the names of the people that were with us, but some of them joined us at the village of Blace.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time Mr. Kuljanin, there were about 30 of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Less, I think. There were less than 30.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Along the way, you met with a number of TO ambushes which you tried to avoid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when you met up with this other group in the village of Blace, you decided, all of you, to head for Kalinovik, reckoning that the road leading to Kalinovik was safer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However on that road too near the village of Ljuta, somebody fired at you so you scattered and fled towards Nerveta and Zara Mrkajic got lost and separated from the group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That was the time when you captured the TO member whom you referred you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The man was captured later when he happened to run into us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then you took his M48 from him, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That boy promised to take you to Kalinovik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you led you for 2 or 3 kilometres?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And about 3 kilometres before reaching the village of Ljuta you captured 2 more TO members?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we captured the young boy we separated into two groups and the second group, which I was not a part of, they were the ones who probably captured those army members, but I am not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I remind you that the young man you captured was called Dzevlan?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I say Karadzic Sucro, does that mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I only know the young man that we captured whom I can remember his face, but I do not recall his name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The first to enter the village of Ljuta was Zara Mrkajic and he was captured there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He entered the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And he called you to come down into the village as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in the village you met with Mirsad Fisic known as Kolombo, a member of the TO, who also promised to take you to Kalinovik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea what his name was or who he was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you know that a TO member put you up in the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was not one member, there were several members.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And they treated you correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until they locked us up in the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But Mr. Kuljanin, you can surely confirm that some people from your group were not brought to the school in the village of Ljuta but that in the process of fleeing, they managed to cross over into Serb controlled territory. Let me give you the names, Mitar Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Counsel please, take it more slowly so that the interpreters can get it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I keep warning others but I myself forget often. Mr. Kuljanin, until you were put up in the school, there was no mistreatment, you were given correct treatment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until the school.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, in the course of the night just before dawn some other persons entered the school, not those you had surrendered to, and then your troubles began?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some of them said that Juko Karadzic, a TO member, had been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you do know that one of the three captured persons, Juko, Karadzic was killed on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only know of one person captured. I do not know about the other two, nor am I familiar with the killing of anyone, because the group I was in did not come across those two people, nor did it kill anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, I will not ask you about your crossing over Bjeljasinca by truck to Konjic as you have told us about that in detail during the examination-in-chief. Your honours, I apologise. I do not know whether this is an error, but I am being told that the list of names which was confirmed by the witness does not appear in the transcript, so is that a mistake or will the names be added subsequently?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: It was the period when you were so fast that the interpreter could not get the names accurately. If you still want to return to it, perhaps you might repeat the question and go back to it so that it will be correctly recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, I will do that. Mr. Kuljanin, I have already asked you but in view of the fact that your answer has not been fully recorded in the transcript, will you please confirm it once again, that the group of about 30 people included the following people, a group that you were in and that was heading for Kalinovik. Mirko Dordic, Dragan Vujcic, Kulas from Tarcin, whose name I do not know, Veko from Tarcin, Zara Mrkajic, Branislav Gligorevic, Milovan Gligorevic, Momir Mrkajic, Jelenko Milosevic, Rajko Kuljanin, Jelenko Kuljanin, Velimir Kuljanin, Mitar Kuljanin, known as Mico, Milorad Kuljanin, Milovan Kuljanin, Snjezan Gligorevic, Mladen Gligorevic, known as Hasko, Radjov Zivak, Aleksa Gligorevic. Will you please confirm, is this part of the group that was moving with you towards Kalinovik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you have confirmed that some persons from the group got separated and whom you did not see later on and who were not brought to the school in Ljuta, will you please confirm whether they are the following persons: Mitar Kuljanin, Mladen Gligorevic, known as Hasko Snjezan Gligorevic, Milorad Kuljanin, Milovan Kuljanin, Zdravko Zuza and Jako from Tarcin; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I apologise, your Honours, I shall do my best when such important things at least are in question that I speak slowly and clearly so that everyone can follow. Mr. Kuljanin, you did not know the persons who arrested you; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not know the persons either who took you aboard the vehicle from the place of Ljuta to Bjelasnica and later on to Konjic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These are people that you did not know from Konjic, your native town?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not know those people who took us from Ljuta and from Igman to the Celebici camp, that is correct, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kuljanin, if everything which I have just asked you and what you have confirmed stands in the statement which you gave to the military investigative commission in Celebici in the way in which you have answered me, then that is correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If what I have just now asked you, or rather to put it better your answers to my questions are contained also in the statement which you made in Celebici, then that part of the statement is correct, is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, I do not know what stands in the statement, but what you have just read to me now is correct. I have just confirmed that that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask now, with the assistance of the usher, for you to be shown the statement of June 8th, which the proposal of my learned colleague Mr. Ackerman was admitted yesterday as evidence, 15 D4. In the Bosnian language, please. (Handed). Mr. Kuljanin, I shall not ask you about the content of the statement. Please take a look at the top of the statement. Is it true that it reads: "Good for co-operation", or "co-operative", on the top of the first page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can see those words.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would also like to ask you to see whether it is 1K written there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That could be the mark of the category to which you have been assigned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea what that means.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew, Mr. Kuljanin, that the first category of prisoners was that category which was considered to be the more difficult category?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: How can this difficult category be prisoners who are co-operative? I fail to see that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer to that question. We shall have to ask some of the members of the commission.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer either.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think it would be helpful if the witness could be reminded to wait for the translation before he answers. It is starting to all run together. Even though Ms. Residovic is moving slowly, the witness is answering immediately rather than waiting for the translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So we have the same warning as the one I gave yesterday, so please be so kind as to wait for the translation of my question and to answer me only then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should like to ask you, Mr. Kuljanin, also to take a look at the top of the first page . There are two signatures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the last page of the statement, also there are two identical signatures; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I remind you in order to refresh your memory a bit, can you, on the basis of these signatures, remember that your interrogation was conducted by Mr. Sacir Pajic and Mr. Nusret Secibovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea who interrogated me, nor did I know those people, nor did I know them then.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This exhibit can be returned. Mr. Kuljanin, after Rajko Dordic called you to come down to Ljuta, members of the TO first ask that one of you should collect the weapons and surrender them to TO members; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I did not understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you, when you came down, surrender those weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You did not even hand over the rifle that you had taken from the member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had no rifle, so I had nothing to surrender.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But before this court, you have said that your group had disarmed a member of the TO and taken his rifle from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I stated that he had been disarmed and a rifle had been seized from him. In fact, I said it was taken by the members of the other group.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So if a third person were to say that on that occasion you surrendered 24 pieces of automatic and other weapons, that party according to your memory would not be saying the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you stated that there were 30 of us in the group, and that 24 of us had surrendered the weapons and now you enumerated a list of the people in the second group, of which there were 15, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So the mistake could be in the number of weapons concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea neither regarding the weapons or the person who surrendered the rifle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, okay, I will not ask you about the weapons any more, you have been asked enough about that subject. You have known Mr. Rajko Dordic from before; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very slightly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you did know that he was working for the Territorial Defence headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I only knew that he was working somewhere in Konjic and that --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And that he resided in Konjic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you saw Mr. Rajko Dordic in April and May in Bradina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did when he came home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The battles in Bradina lasted until May 27th; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know about the combat. I do not know how long the attack lasted. I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The attack was still going on when you left Bradina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Muslim units were setting fire to houses and killing civilians in the village called Suljina Strana. Before they advanced to the centre we started to pull out from the encirclement that we were in.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when you were taken to Konjic to the Drustveni Dom to the social centre, Zilic ordered that all your things and documents be seized; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And everything was taken away from you except from the things which you managed to hide?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Documents, your identity card, your watch was taken away from you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my papers and some other documents, my ID -- I did not have an ID.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have stated before that in Celebici, during the first few weeks, you used to see soldiers with HBO insignia and the military police HBO insignia as well as with lilies insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall having stated that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If this were contained in the statement which you gave to the investigator then it would not be correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have replied to questions regarding the statement which I have signed many times and I do not wish to comment upon what is contained there any more. I do not subscribe to that statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned colleague, Mr. Ackerman, has asked you in connection with that particular statement whether the investigator of the Prosecution had warned you at the time that some of those people had been indicted and you confirmed that you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not understood. What have I confirmed as correct?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That when making that statement, you had been warned that Mr. Delalic, Mucic, Landzo and Delic had been indicted and you confirmed that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What did I confirm?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That you had been warned of that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You gave that statement in October 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that these persons were indicted only in March 1996?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea when.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you claim that the investigator of the Prosecution, if he told you that, gave you false data?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I do not care very much about their indictments so I did not remember the dates which he mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kuljanin, you were not interested at all whether on the basis of your statement some people could be indicted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not even today am I interested in these indictments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something in connection with your stay in tunnel 9. Please tell me whether it is true that you reach the door of tunnel 9 by a small assent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that after entering tunnel number 9, it has a slight gradient sloping towards the end of the tunnel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That would mean that the door of the tunnel are at sort of the top of this decline or ascent of this entire space?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From the door, the tunnel goes downward?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, is it true that in a space of about a metre from the door of this tunnel, there was some kind of a bucket or container with water or some vessels with water in which you received your food?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let me refresh your memory. Please pay attention. Is it true that after this space there sat prisoners in tunnel number 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they sat there, the prisoners sat there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As it was a narrow tunnel two people could not sit facing each other, they had to sit one next to the other in a row; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As far as you remember, the first sitting next to this space was Mirko Mrkajic called Bruba?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he came several days, I do not remember how many days, after us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Next to him was sitting his son Velimir known as Vele; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And the third next to him was sitting Desimir Mrkajic about whom you talked yesterday with my colleague Ackerman; is that so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And next to him Velibor Mrkajic was sitting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you already mentioned Velibor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: No, that was Velimir, Vele and this one is Velibor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then Brane Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Bradko Kuljanin was the next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in front of you was Nikola Mrkajic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then you yourself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And then followed Andelko Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And so on. Let me not enumerate all the rest. So my information is correct on the basis of what we have heard so far from the witnesses about the exact sequence of the people seated in the tunnel in the way in which you have just now confirmed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So you were the ninth person sitting in this row?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If perhaps in the course of the hitherto interrogation you did say something different, that is because it is hard to remember all the facts after the lapse of so much time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let us now go back to the question of your final departure from Konjic. I shall ask you again whether criminal proceedings had been instituted against you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of having been abolished?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you told us yesterday, you were neither liberated nor exchanged, but you fled?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But why would I have to be pardoned or criminally prosecuted? From whom did I need abolition or pardon, why?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, yesterday we discussed in depth this situation. The process is such that I put the questions and you answer my questions. It is not your business to ask me questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was just answering your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Actually, on November 3rd 1994 or 1993, I beg your pardon, yes 1993, of course, with a group of prisoners, you overpowered a TO member, captured his weapon, seized his weapon, and together with him, reached Croatian territory, or rather territory under the control of Croatian forces where you felt you were quite safe?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We reached the territory halfway between Croat and Muslim territory and then he went back home.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you had known this person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had not, I knew him as one of the guards in the prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He was Salko Bilanovic, is that not so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think his name was Salko, I do not know his surname.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you know he was killed later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me make this clear. Salko came with us, as I had already said, until we reached a territory that was halfway between Croat and Muslim territory. Salko treated us correctly in the prison, that is true. It is also true that we did disarm him and seized his rifle, but we spoke as normal people and we said goodbye normally. Of course we did not dare give him back his rifle and Salko left. What happened to him I learnt only much later from other prisoners when they were released from the Musala camp. As far as we were concerned, Salko was released and treated quite normally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that you said that a doctor had appeared and carried out an examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, I heard that from prisoners in the Musala camp and they said that it was probably his heart or something, that the doctors had established that he had died from his heart attack or heart failure.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But it is true that Salko Bilanovic, after your escape, did not return to Konjic alive?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He did not return, but it is not true that we killed him. I already told you why he did not return.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Kuljanin, that you and your group were under suspicion of having killed this person; is that true?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were under suspicion by certain people who know nothing about anything, and then the doctor came and the commander of the camp came and said what had happened. The commander knew him and I was close to him even before the war. He told the other prisoners that we had not killed him, that the truth is so and so, that it was heart failure he had suffered from.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Kuljanin, in a rather strange way, you were suspected twice, once of having killed a TO member at the village of Ljuta whom you had disarmed and captured and then again when escaping that you had killed the person who you had overpowered and disarmed, even though that is not true.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is not true, this is the first I hear from you that I was a suspect. If I had been suspected, surely criminal proceedings would have been conducted against me in the Musala camp itself, as was the case with some other people who were taken to trial even while I was at the Musala camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But you know that both Salko Bilanovic and Karadzic -- let me just find his name -- that these persons are dead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I heard of Bilanovic, for the other person that you mentioned, I do not know whether you mentioned him first or second, anyway in the village of Ljuta I had no idea about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Suko Karcic. So you have no idea about him? Very well then, thank you. I have only a few more brief questions to put to you. Mr. Kuljanin, you said that before the war you were not a SDS member?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not. I was not a member of the SDS at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Fine, but as a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the former Yugoslavia, you know that people were highly sensitive to certain insignia from the Second World War which were reminiscent of the crimes committed during that war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew that it was very badly seen to carry insignia with the letter U because they represented the Ustashas and the special cockard hats that were a symbol of the Chetniks, did you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Both these had committed very serious crimes during the Second World War, had they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not participate in the Second World War, so I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you did not study about it in history?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not a very good pupil. If I had studied history, I probably would not have been in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So because you did not study history and because you were not familiar with this, frequently before the war broke out, you wore various signs on your cap?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never in my life, madam. I went to the camp and have left the camp and never in my life did I put any kind of signs on my clothes and I would like anyone to come and tell me in my face that they had seen me wearing any kind of signs of this kind. I have no reason to find excuses. If I had worn a cockade, I would admit it before this honourable court, but that, madam, is simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I am asking you, it is up to you to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have answered you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That is why you were seen in cafes wearing a pistol and also singing Chetnik songs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, you are misinformed 100 per cent. If I had sang such songs, I would not conceal the fact. I would like to have a drink and who drinks usually also since.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But if you did sing such songs and carry such insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Madam, I cannot say that. I cannot say that I have never sang a song now and then, but I can say I never sung such songs before the war or during the war, before the camp or after the camp madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But your behaviour, and even if you drank and sang Chetnik songs, would provoke misunderstanding and cause difficulties with representatives of other ethnic groups and the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Objection, your Honour, asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I believe you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never, madam, did I wear any kind of insignia or signs and it would appear from what you are saying that all I did was sing, that I never did any work at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your honours, my question -- my first question was whether this provoked misunderstanding amongst members of other ethnic groups and the police.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Never did I have any problems with my neighbours, with members of other ethnic groups, or the police for that sort of thing. I never had any difficulties with the police on account of nationalism and I was very good, I had very good relations with my neighbours from the very first day. What happened later on we have all seen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuljanin. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Kuljanin, I am just going to be fairly short with you I hope, because I think quite a lot of the ground has already been covered. Can I ask you please to start off and just tell us a little more about the military service you did between 1987 and 1989. You were in the military police. What rank did you end up with please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a soldier, I had no rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Apart from being in the military police, did you receive ordinary infantry training, prior to going into the police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I did my military service and when training like any other soldier, the normal training that anybody was given in the military service at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Basic training in how to be a soldier, how to be an infantry man, before going on into the military police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: All this was happening in the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You ceased to be in the military police in 1989. Thereafter, did you remain fit and healthy until the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In 1992, that was just, what, three years after you had completed your military service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: All that you had been taught and all you had learnt in the military police, all that was still fresh in your mind at the time, was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your evidence is that you took no part in any fighting of any kind, nor were you recruited to any militia or anything like that, despite the fact that you had recent military service, is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is it, but I did my military service because I had to, and I served in the police not because I wanted to do it but because I had to do it; it was an obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Did you carry out any military service after your escape in 1994, Mr. Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not for a single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I want to turn now to the circumstances in which you made your statement to the Office of the Prosecution. That was in October 1995, Mr. Kuljanin. You have been asked about it, you recall the man who was interviewing you was called Ole Hortemo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Help us about this: how was it that you came to be interviewed by the office of the Prosecution? How did they get in touch with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have no idea how they got in touch with me. We spoke on the telephone, we made an appointment. At first I did not know what it was about. When I got there, they told me what it was about. I did not have enough time because I had to rush back to work and that is how we got in touch.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: What was your work at that time, Mr. Kuljanin, in October 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working in a company as a machine operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: But you spent, what, two complete days with Mr. Hortemo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two days, yes, but a few minutes, that is the question. Each day I could spend maybe so many minutes, a certain limited amount of time anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the rush that you have described to us was not personal business, but you just had to get back to work, was that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had to go to work. Nobody else could work instead of me. In that sense, it was private.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just help us about this. You have told us yesterday that you recall having had a further visit from some people after 20th and 21st October 1995. Do you remember telling us about that yesterday?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were some other visits but I was not very keen about the whole thing. I had not intended to appear in the Tribunal in this honourable court, so I did not pay very close attention to the whole thing, nor was I prepared to make any detailed statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You say visits; there was more than one visit, was there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, somebody came twice to put questions to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Was that somebody from the office of the Prosecution or from some other body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably from the Prosecution, as far as I can recall. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Having answered some questions, did you put anything down in writing and sign it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that I did sign what I had stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That being so, I would invite the Prosecution to say whether they have any other statement from this man that they have so far not disclosed concerning this man's evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is it now you are asking for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We can say, your Honour, that we have only one statement which was the one which was disclosed actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you. I am grateful to my learned friend for that information. Mr. Kuljanin, let us move on please if we may. I want to ask you now about the incidents you described to us yesterday concerning the war and your detention and your escape. That took a period of your life of about two and a half years, would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And in general terms, would you agree with this, that those events were the most significant set of events in your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Most significant? I did not want the war, I did not want the camp, I did not want any of it. It happened. What I experienced is what I had wanted least, so that I do not consider it significant. It cost me my life and my health. I do not see for whom that could be considered significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Perhaps another word might help you. The most memorable incident of your life, Mr. Kuljanin; would you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember too well and I want to forget everything I experienced and I survived and I am turning to other matters. I want to start another life. I am no longer interested in Bosnia or anything related to that, not even the camp in which I spent so much time.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: No doubt, Mr. Kuljanin, but just for the moment, for the next 20 minutes or so you are going to be here answering questions and I would like you to help me if you can please. You understand how important it is, the evidence that you are giving, do you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It depends for whom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let us just ask you about this. I want to ask you about the incident where you claim to have been locked up in a manhole, Mr. Kuljanin. Would you agree with this, that that is one of the most serious incidents that occurred to you during your detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was serious, whether it was the most serious I do not know. It is difficult to measure. There were various incidents and terrible experiences.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: If your account is right, you and several other people were close to death from asphyxiation, were you not, Mr. Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No -- yes, I was close to death every day and also in the manhole.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Something of which you have a clear memory; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Something you are going to remember for the rest of your life?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if I will remember it for the rest of my life. It is only now that my memories have been refreshed, since I have been visiting here with the Prosecution and the court, otherwise I do not remember too well and I want to forget it as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You see, I suggest to you, Mr. Kuljanin, that it was so serious an incident you could not possibly have forgotten it, even if you were in a hurry or in a dilemma about whether you would give evidence or not; is that right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not forgotten it completely, but I am doing my best to get over it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You did not mention it in your statement when you were trying your best to remember things for Mr. Hortemo, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I did not remember everything, maybe there are many other things that I should have said but I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let us go through a few of those things, Mr. Kuljanin. The visit of the film crew that you described to us yesterday. Another major incident during the course of your detention, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Why did you not mention that in your statement when you were speaking to Mr. Hortemo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said how little time I had with him and I spent 18 months in the camp. How can I be expected to tell him everything within half a hour? Is that possible? That is not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: For example, the two incidents you describe of stealing food with Mr. Mucic; again not mentioned in your statement, was it, Mr. Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely it was not mentioned but I lived through it and I experienced it and participated in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Tell us a little bit about that incident. Did Mr. Mucic take you off in the vehicle on his own to deliver the food wherever it was going?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he drove the van himself to his house, to the destination where we unloaded the food which he provided for his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And he was on his own on both occasions, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he drove the car, we went in that we had loaded.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Bearing in mind your escape in 1994, why did you not escape on that occasion if you only had Mr. Mucic to deal with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was in the centre of the town, I escaped from the frontline where it was much easier, much simpler. It was impossible to escape in these other circumstances, even though he was alone and there were four of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Let us move on to another incident that you did not mention in your statement, the incident where you saw Mr. Mucic making up a list for transfer of prisoners and the actual transfer of those prisoners. You did not mention that in your statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not mention it because I did not remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And the incident in which you described to us yesterday, your meeting with Mr. Delalic and going to his home and doing some work there; you did not mention that either, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not say I had met with Mr. Delalic, I said something quite different regarding Mr. Delalic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: You know the incident to which I am referring, do you not, Mr. Kuljanin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The incident that occurred in front of his house, yes. I did not say that I had met Mr. Delalic, I never stated that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: I am sorry for having misled you and I apologise for that, but you know which one we are talking about. You did not put that in your statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not. I have already given the reason why. I had little time at my disposal and one needs much more time to remember everything, and even now I did not mention all the things that may have occurred to me overnight and this morning, even.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: And your interrogation at the camp, again something you did not mention in your statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The visit of the Red Cross, again something that you did not mention in your statement, did you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not mention it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: In fact the only mention that you make concerning Mr. Mucic in your statement was this, that he was the commander for the first ten months in Celebici. Now Mr. Kuljanin, you were not even --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know for how many months, I just know that he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: That is what you put in your statement, Mr. Kuljanin. You were not even in Celebici for ten months, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? I did not understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: It is a quite simple question, Mr. Kuljanin. You were not in Celebici camp for ten months, were you? It was only a matter of four months.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but he was in Musala too, he was in charge of Musala too. I was in Musala.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Nor do the Prosecution suggest, as I confirmed with Mr. Turone yesterday, that he was the commander for more than six months, Mr. Kuljanin. I suggest to you that the only fact which you recorded in your statement concerning Mr. Mucic was one that was wholly incorrect, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: The one single statement that you made about Mr. Mucic in your witness statement to Mr. Hortemo was one that you got wrong, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still do not understand what is not correct, what is wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Mr. Mucic was not commander for ten months, that is what you got wrong, Mr. Kuljanin, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was about -- I do not know exactly how long I was in the camp, but when I was transferred to Musala, Mr. Mucic came there and he formed lists of people and he was carrying a list, what kind of list it was I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kuljanin. I am grateful to my learned friend for just reminding me of one point. You say that Mr. Mucic's house was in the centre of Konjic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the centre, in the very centre, but it was in the broader area of the town of Konjic. I was not so specific, I do not have a map to tell you exactly where his house was. Konjic was not such a big city, it was all near, everything was near.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: How close to the centre of Konjic? Within a kilometre?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Just remind us of the date when you were transferred to Musala camp, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I just do not know the date, I am sorry, I do not remember dates very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Would you accept December 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think so, November/December roughly. I just cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Kuljanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, a housekeeping matter, I do not think anyone moved to introduce the OTP statement yesterday. I provided the Registry with a copy of it and I move to introduce the statement that this witness gave to the Office of the Prosecutor for the limited purpose of impeachment only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I thought it was introduced on behalf of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, your Honour, the other two statements that he gave were. Nobody ever got around to moving the introduction of the OTP statement. That is what I am doing now, again, just for the limited purpose of impeachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which statement is that? Let me have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know if it has a number, but it is the one with the OTP cover sheet on it, dated 20th and 21st October 1995. I believe the only two statements that were provided to the court yesterday were the records of his interrogation by the Army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, also the statement refers to two attachments which I do not have, one of them is a diagram of the way people were seated in the camp and the other is a record of some physical examinations that he says he attached and I do not have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Will you kindly help us?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no objection to show the extent to which the witness has and has not been impeached. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Mr. Moran, you cannot directly put it and admit it as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we did yesterday and he admitted it was his statement. I would be happy to do it again. It is exhibit number ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: If the usher would take that to the witness and he could identify his signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us have it numbered appropriately.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be numbered D8/3.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have just been handed one that does apparently have the diagrams on it. It does have a few other markings on it. Would the court like to substitute that? It has a couple of diagrams on it, no medical records. We can substitute that one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Is this one which the court has? The one I have has no diagrams on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe this one is more complete than the one I was provided it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Why do we have two different types?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do not know, I just got the one out of my file box that had this witness's name on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Which of them is the OTP statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: They are both the OTP statement, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: We have a complete copy, if your honours wish, of the English statements with the attachment which were drawn by the witness in front of the investigator and we can provide that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we move to substitute that one and let him identify the one that is in Mr. Turone's hand. Mr. Kuljanin, if you just look at that piece of paper that the usher is about set to hand you, is that your signature on those documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: There is no translation coming through at the present time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: And that is a true and correct copy of the statement you gave to the Office of the Prosecutor in October 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have already said in connection with this statement that I did not make it exhaustive, I did not remember all the facts when I made that statement. I have repeated this several times. I do not mind, I can go on repeating it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: No, sir, all we are trying to do is just to guarantee the copy that you are identifying right now is in fact a true and correct copy of whatever you did in October 1995. We are just basically proving that the document is authentic. Your Honour with that, I would move to introduce for the limited purposes of impeachment only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: All right. I think the Prosecution wants it admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be exhibit D8/3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Do you have any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Just a clarification coming out from the cross-examination done by Mr. Ackerman yesterday. Mr. Kuljanin, one of the Defence lawyers yesterday, Mr. Ackerman, asked you some questions about your knowledge of Mr. Landzo's first name. He showed you your OTP statement, this one, where you referred to Mr. Landzo with the first name of Senad. You said that in fact you did not know for sure Mr. Landzo's first name, but you said it might be Senad, so in order to clear up any confusion over this matter, I would ask you to look around in this courtroom and see in this courtroom whether the person that you are referring to in your evidence as Landzo is present in this room. Please look around and see if you see Mr. -- the person you name as Mr. Landzo in this room?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I actually object to that. There is no way he could fail to make that identification. It is of absolutely no relevance whatsoever. It is obvious that there are certain persons sitting in the dock here, I think it is totally inappropriate to make an identification like that, therefore I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I respond this as a question of re-examination? It comes out from the cross-examination of yesterday. By the way, in yesterday's transcript on page 5541, Mr. Ackerman said exactly: "Your position here today is that as far as you know, the person named Landzo who did the things that you have described, was a person named Senad Landzo; correct? Answer: I repeat, I am not sure about the name, the first name. I am sure about the surname and his face and his physical appearance. That I am sure of." So as your Honour said, quite often the cross-examining party has to bear the consequences of cross-examination. On the other hand, the objection of Mr. Ackerman goes to weight, not admissibility. May I please ask the witness to answer this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GREAVES
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a matter of general importance, in my submission. This is a process known in my jurisdiction, and I suspect those of others in the common law system, as what is called a dock identification. In the 1970s, as a result of a number of cases involving identification evidence, the process of dock identification came under scrutiny by the legal system in the United Kingdom. As a result of that, Her Majesty's Attorney General announced that because dock identifications were so inherently and fundamentally unreliable and dangerous, no Prosecutor would be permitted from that day forward to carry out that exercise in a court in the United Kingdom. I respectfully submit that the point made by my learned friend, Mr. Ackerman, is an entirely proper one. It is a dangerous proceeding and one which should not be permitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I see no danger in it at all. The witness is very familiar with the person he is talking about. If there is any ambiguity, he is entitled to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: May I invite you to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Let us hear from the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had said that I was not sure and I still do not know his real first name, but I know his surname and I know the nickname that was used in the camp itself. Yesterday, I said, I do not know whether you heard me, that I could recognise him and that I know him well and it is absolutely no difficulty for me to recognise him among the accused and point a finger at him. As for his name, I again say I am not sure. I think that was his name, I did not know. I could have found out his real name, but I was not interested. As for his physical appearance and his description, I can easily show, point a finger, to Landzo called Zenga, for the benefit of your honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Please do that, point him out.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Landzo Zenga (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: Do you mean the person sitting on which?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between the two policemen (indicates).

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: For the record, may we -- let the record reflect that the witness identified the accused. All right, Mr. Kuljanin, just to make quite clear, is the person that you pointed to now, is this person the one you have been talking about yesterday as the person who beat you and did many other things which you referred to as Landzo, the Landzo who was in Celebici?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Absolutely so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TURONE
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, my re-examination is finished. Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: I think the end of this witness's evidence. Thank you very much for your assistance. The Trial Chamber will now rise and I think re-assemble at 12.10. (11.40 am) (A short break) (12.15 pm)

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, your Honour, before the next witness is called, I have a little housekeeping matter I would like to bring to the court's attention. Back on 24th July or thereabouts, I received in my office, and I think the rest of the Defence lawyers received by telecopy a letter from Mr. Niemann setting out who witnesses were going to be and the order in which they were going to be called. This morning we received another list from Mr. Niemann which, although it is similar to the list of July 24th, there are some significant differences in it, and the list we got this morning is substantially longer. I have copies of those for the Tribunal, if you would like to take a look at them. The only thing I would request, I understand that the Prosecution may have problems lining up witnesses and making sure who is going to be where when they are supposed to be there, just as I am sure those of us on the Defence side will have the same problem, but when you are given notice from the Prosecutor that says: "Below please find the witnesses we expect to call during the two week court session, please be advised this proposal is based on our current assessment of availability." You prepare for that, you start beginning preparing for these witnesses, and then when at 10 o'clock in the morning you are handed another list that is somewhat different and in fact includes the names of witnesses that the Trial Chamber has not authorised the Prosecution to call, it affects our preparation, and again, we understand that the Prosecution have some problems, but your Honour, we would like to just bring this to the court's attention and ask, if we get something, let us stick to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much, except my first appeal to counsel on both sides, because this is a matter which need not even come before the Trial Chamber, these are things you could have thrashed out, because you all have identical difficulties in getting witnesses and arranging, prosecution or defence. All you need is to have a joint view as to how this case has to go on. I am sorry this is appearing to affect how you would respond to whoever is called as a witness. Obviously that has to be, but I think Mr. Niemann might have some explanation to this, because it is a little difficult on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. It seems to me that it is unfortunate that counsel could not discuss it with us first. Difficulties like that can sometimes be resolved rather than making it a matter for your honours to have to deal with. If that is the way it is to be, that is the way it is to be. Your Honour, the situation is that we are unfortunately in a very flexible and liquid situation where it is not easy to -- fluid situation where it is not easy for us to be as definite as one would be in a national jurisdiction where we have powers of ensuring that people can be brought before the court under pain of penalty. Regrettably we are not in that position and we do not have that luxury. People do decide at the last moment either not to come forward or whatever. Indeed, it reaches situations where people simply say "I am not coming this week because I am attending some function and too bad". When confronted with those sorts of problems, it makes it very hard for us to apply rigid procedures which would obviously make the Defence work easier, and no doubt they will experience a similar thing, but hopefully when they are confronted with a similar problem they can raise it with us and we will endeavour to try and co-operate with the problems that they are going to face in the same way as we have faced them. Insofar as unauthorised lists are concerned, unauthorised witnesses, that may be the case, your Honour, but the situation is that we are giving the Defence notice. If your honours decide they are not to be called, obviously those witnesses will fall off the list, but the Defence cannot be heard then to complain that they were not given the list of witnesses that we anticipated to call in anticipation of your Honour's decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Actually what is being complained about here is perhaps the precipitation by which this change was caused. If they are given some time they will know how to adjust or discuss it with you. Whether it has been authorised or not authorised, you know how to meet the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour. That is the reason why we gave the list, including unauthorised witnesses so they are on notice. I wish I could say here now that the list will not change. Sadly, that is not the luxury of this jurisdiction, your Honour. It is a very fluid and changeable situation and we unfortunately, all of us, suffer from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MORAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so the record is clear, although this Trial Chamber issued an order yesterday having to do with some of the witnesses, the court will recall that at least on behalf of Mr. Delic, we had no objection to the prosecution calling whoever they wanted to call. We had no objection to them adding to their witness list.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your honours, I should like to subscribe to the argumentation stated by my learned colleague, but I do have to emphasise that the list which we got this morning contains 21 names, of which a significant number differs from the list which we received seven days ago. I believe that that, despite the problems, the Prosecutor's side would have to have, for the Defence, a number of witnesses, a list of the number of witnesses which will be invited so that we can prepare ourselves in advance, because on the basis of the list that we received on 24th July, we prepared ourselves unnecessarily for some of them. Also, there are nine persons on the list which we received this morning which were never on the Prosecutor's list, and on the basis of the decision of yesterday, which we received yesterday, it has not been yet decided whether they will feature on the list at all. Now we do not know whether the court will at all admit these people being summoned as witnesses, but we have to exert maximum efforts on our side to prepare ourselves for the witnesses so that we have to know, I comprehend the problems which occurred in the month of May, but four months after this time, I believe that the court should ask the Prosecution side to give us a total list, because the Defence, in view of the needs of its investigators in the field and in view of its necessary preparations, should have to be informed on time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hate to continue this discussion, but I do want to rise to say that I subscribe to everything Mr. Niemann has told you in terms of the problems they are having and agree that we are probably going to have the same kinds of problems. I suppose that if anything, what we are all trying to say to the court and probably could have been said just as easily to Mr. Niemann directly, is that the fear that we have is that all of a sudden a witness is going to pop into the courtroom without us having adequate notice and time to prepare cross-examination. I would think that at least 48 hours would be a reasonable time to have notice and perhaps even more than that, depending upon whether it is a witness we have known about for a long time or not. I think that is the concern that is being expressed. I do not think it is a technical matter about lists and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLUJIC
utterances.text: Your honours, I fully subscribe to what my distinguished and learned colleagues have just said, but perhaps I should also like to draw the attention of the distinguished prosecution to the fact that in May and June, during this process, the prosecution should know -- we are in the fifth or sixth month of this process and the prosecution should know what its complete list should be. We want to have a complete list. We are completely aware that we have a lot of work to do and that we will have a lot of work to do in connection with some witnesses which will perhaps not be heard in this court in view of all the objective circumstances which my learned colleague Niemann has already mentioned, but we want to have a systematic preparation of our Defence possible, so I should like to appeal on our distinguished colleagues on the opposite side to provide us with a complete list, with the risk being involved that perhaps not all those witnesses will also be present at this court. In that case, we shall be able to proceed in a normal way without this nervousness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KARIBI-WHYTE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.
